newsitem.title: CHINA: North Korea main threat, U.S. officer warns China.
newsitem.headline: North Korea main threat, U.S. officer warns China.

text.p: Top U.S. military officer General John Shalikashvili on Wednesday warned China its long-time communist ally North Korea was the greatest threat to peace in the Asia-Pacific region.

Washington was committed to remaining a regional power and was ready for possible conflict on the Korean peninsula, said Shalikashvili, chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, in a speech to China's National Defence University.

North Korea's economic crisis and the apparent inability of the isolated Stalinist nation to feed its people had helped make it the most dangerous factor in Asian-Pacific relations, he said in a prepared copy of the speech released by U.S. diplomats.

"First, and most threatening, is the unpredictable regime in Pyongyang, which poses a major threat to peace on the Korean peninsula and in the surrounding area," said Shalikashvili, the most senior U.S. military officer to visit Beijing since 1983.
China has been long been one of Pyongyang's closest allies. Chinese soldiers fought alongside their North Korean comrades against U.S.-led United Nations forces during the 1950-53 Korean civil war.
Analysts say Beijing remains Pyongyang's most important ally, although ties have cooled since China established diplomatic relations with capitalist South Korea in 1992.

Washington welcomed China's efforts to reduce tensions between the rival Koreas and appreciated Beijing's efforts to reduce tensions on the divided peninsula, said Shalikashvili, who is in the Chinese capital to boost Sino-U.S. military ties.

He told students and staff at the defence university, the academic centre of China's three-million-strong People's Liberation Army, that the United States was also worried by aspects of Beijing's military policies.
Arms sales to Pakistan and Iran were sources of concern, as were Beijing's harsh rhetoric and military actions during presidential elections on Taiwan in March 1996, he said.

Chinese war games and missile tests in the seas near Taiwan prompted Washington to send two aircraft carrier battlegroups to the area in a show of U.S. naval might to ensure the historic polls proceeded undisturbed.
Chinese leaders say Taiwan, Beijing's rival since it became the refuge of defeated Nationalist forces in 1949, is the most sensitive issue affecting long-strained cross-Pacific ties.
Washington wanted more Sino-U.S. exchanges and a military maritime and air cooperation agreement that would cut the risk of miscalculations, Shalikashvili said.

Relations between the world's most powerful military machine and the largest army have slowly revived in recent years since being frozen in 1989 after Chinese soldiers crushed pro-democracy protests in Beijing with heavy loss of life.

"To be a fruitful form of engagement, our military-to-military contacts must deepen and become more frequent, more balanced and more developed," said Shalikashvili, who promised to supply China with details of the U.S. military's equipment and its global deployment.

Information exchange should be more equal, China's military should take part in multinational activities and a regular dialogue between senior military leaders should be introduced, he said, adding that improving contacts would be difficult.

"If we listen to the suspicious side of our military minds, if we don't pursue exchanges on a fair and equitable basis, if we lack openness, transparency, or reciprocity, or if we hold back even routine information on our military forces, then we will fail," he said.
